files.text:
Ravenna · Constantinople

Gold under glass

A gold tessera is a sandwich. The glassmaker poured out a cake of molten glass, usually with a little green or amber in it, and while it was still warm laid a leaf of gold across it, beaten so thin that a breath would lift it. Over the leaf went a second skin of clear glass, much thinner, which Italian workshops still call the cartellina, the little card: sometimes blown as a bubble and cut open, sometimes poured. The whole was put back in the furnace until the two glasses fused and the gold was sealed between them, safe from the air and from a thousand years of lamp smoke. When it had cooled, the cake was set on a small iron blade fixed in a block, the hardie, and broken with a hammer into cubes about the size of a fingernail. Every cube in the vaults of Ravenna and Constantinople went under that hammer one at a time.

The setters worked a patch at a time, as much wet lime plaster as they could fill before it went hard, over a drawing brushed onto the coat beneath. They pressed each cube in with a thumb, and they did not press them flat. In a gold ground the cubes lean, forward, back, to one side, none quite in line with its neighbour, and the joints between them are left open so that each one meets the light by itself. High in a vault the field was often tipped down toward the floor, where the people stood. None of this survives in a photograph, which is taken in one light from one place. It is a surface made for an eye that moves.

In Hagia Sophia, in the thirteenth century, the setters laid the ground behind this face in overlapping fans, like the scales of a fish, so that even the empty gold has a grain. Most of these churches face east, and the apse is the first part of them the morning finds. Before sunrise the gold is a dull brown under the lamps. Then a low, level light comes in through the east windows and across the marble floor, and the gold above takes it at a glancing angle from below, the angle the setters tipped it to meet, so that every cube sends a little of the day back down into the church. The night office was timed to end at first light, with the hymn that begins Glory to you who have shown us the light, and its last verses were sung under a vault that was slowly catching. By mid morning the sun is high, the angle has passed, and the gold settles back to a warm and even glow.

It was lit by oil lamps hung on chains and by candles carried in procession, small flames that moved, and by people who moved under them. Walk the length of the nave with a taper and the wall answers cube by cube: one flares and goes out, the next takes it up, and a spark seems to keep pace beside you through the gold, always just ahead. Procopius, describing Justinian's new church in Constantinople, wrote that you would think the place was not lit from outside by the sun, but that the light was born inside it. He was looking at gold that had been set to do exactly that.

# gold-ground A Byzantine gold mosaic that glints the way the real wall does. In Ravenna or Hagia Sophia each gold cube is a tiny mirror set a few degrees off true, so as you walk past, or a candle moves, single cubes flash and go out and a field of separate sparks travels with you. Photographs flatten that away. Here the photograph is only the colour: every real tessera in it was found, given its own tilt and material, and lit again. Scrolling past moves your eye, the pointer carries a candle, and on a phone tilting it moves the eye too. ```html ``` Each image needs its baked tile data beside it, `-tiles.png` (or name it with `data-tiles`). The `` sizes the wall: leave it at its natural ratio, or give the figure a height and the img `object-fit: cover` and any `object-position`; the lighting takes exactly the same crop. Or call `goldGround(figure, options)` yourself; it returns `destroy()`. ## Options | attribute | option | default | | |---|---|---|---| | `data-tiles` | `tiles` | `-tiles.png` | the baked tile data (same origin) | | `data-distance` | `distance` | `2.2` | how far away you stand, in screen sizes; the lights stand off the wall in proportion. Smaller = tighter pools of light that travel faster as you scroll | | `data-candle` | `candle` | `1` | 0-2, the carried candle: it follows the pointer, and without one is held just right of the middle of the screen, so its pool walks along the wall as you scroll | | `data-window` | `window` | `1` | 0-2, a broad window high and to the right, fixed to the church: a second, slower pool | | `data-glow` | `glow` | `0.5` | 0-1, bloom round the brightest sparks; `0` skips the bloom passes | | `data-bloom` | `bloom` | off | arrive greyed and warm into gold as the wall reaches the middle of the screen | The options object wins over the attributes. ## Theming | variable | default | | |---|---|---| | `--gg-floor` | `--paper-2` | behind the image while it loads | `.gg-band` is a full-width strip, `min(92svh, max(52vw, min(72svh, 640px)))` tall, with the image covering it. There is nothing else to theme: the colour is the mosaic's and the light's. ## How it works **Offline: finding the real tesserae.** (Python, scikit-image; the scripts are not shipped.) The grout is a network of thin dark valleys between brighter cubes, so a black-ridge filter (Sato, at the grout's width) is combined with a white-ridge filter (in dark passages, hair and robes, the mortar reads lighter than the glass) and a colour-edge term, each normalised by local contrast. What is left once the joints are removed is the faces of the cubes; their distance transform peaks once in the middle of each cube (h-maxima keeps one peak per oblong cube), and a slightly compact watershed from those seeds fills each cube out to its joints. Checked by drawing the region edges over the photograph and inspecting 3x crops: in the gold ground the edges lie on the real grout, cube by cube (Justinian's band: 21,400 cubes; the Deësis panel: 24,400). Faces, where the cubes are smaller and the photograph softer, are rougher, so they are given almost no specular and no edge shadow. **Classification.** From each cube's median colour: gold (hue 28-64°, saturated, not dark, and inside a gold neighbourhood, so flesh-coloured cubes in a face do not count), silver or leafless glass (pale and unsaturated inside the gold), coloured or dark glass, and stone. **Setting.** Each cube gets a tilt drawn from a 2-D normal distribution: σ ≈ 6° per axis for gold, 5° for silver, 3° for the rest. One cube in twenty was set carelessly steep (σ 15°), and those are the lone sparks that catch far from where the light falls. On top of that comes a systematic downward tip (3° for gold), as in vaults set to meet people standing below. Gold gets smoother surfaces than glass or stone. A cube is **confident** if its region is the size and shape of one cube: between 0.3 and 2.6 times the median area, solidity above 0.82 and eccentricity below 0.95. That holds for 74% of the gold in the band and 86% in the panel. Everything is baked into one lossless RGB PNG at the image's resolution: - R, G: the normal's x and y (128 = straight out, ±127 = ±0.5). - B: material in bits 7-6, confidence in bit 5, roughness in bits 4-0. Neighbouring cubes always get different values, because the shader finds a cube's edges wherever the value changes and so needs no separate edge map. **Light: pools, not stars.** The light is a fragment shader that reads the data nearest-neighbour. - **Curved wall.** The wall is gently concave, like the inside of an apse (radius 8 × the viewing distance), so its surface normal turns slowly across the field. Each cube's own tilt rides on top of that. - **Lights.** The eye is at the middle of the screen. There are two lights: - a candle, carried in screen space: it is at the pointer, or held just right of centre, near the wall; - a broad window that belongs to the church: high and to the right, fixed to the wall. - **The pool.** Each light reflects as a Gaussian lobe on the half-vector. The lobe is about as wide as the spread of the setting (roughness 0.07-0.1, plus the size of the source). So where the mirror angle of the curved wall passes through the setting angle there is a pool: many cubes catch at once, at graded strengths, some full, many half, some dark. Outside it the catches thin out quickly to single steep cubes. - **Movement.** Scrolling moves the wall under you and under the candle, so the candle's pool travels across the gold and breaks up differently cube by cube as it goes. The window's pool slides more slowly. - **Uncertain regions.** A cube that is not confident gets only the pool's averaged light, computed on the wall's own curve with the lobe widened by the tilt spread, so it never flashes as a shard. - **Materials.** - Gold mirrors the light gold-tinted, with a touch of white from the glass skin, so a peak goes nearly white. - Silver only glints where its segmentation is confident. - Coloured glass gets a faint, shapeless gloss on the macro curve; stone gets none. - **Dark gold.** Gold that is not catching is darker and browner than the flash-lit photograph (bright-photographed gold more so). Each cube also reflects a slightly different part of a dim church, so the field is never even. - **Rims.** A cube's rim loses its glint and takes a hair of shadow. - **Bloom.** Highlights roll off to white. The light is computed again at half resolution; only light above 1.05 is kept, blurred twice each way and added back, so the hottest cubes in a pool glow. ## Tuning `data-distance` sets the scale. Lights stand out from the wall at a fraction of it, so a smaller distance gives tighter pools that move faster with scroll; the panel uses `1.2`. Other places to tune: - `setLight()`: - `uCurve`: how fast the wall turns; a smaller radius gives a narrower pool. - The window position, high and to the right of the wall. - The candle's height off the wall. - The shader: - `wr` (lobe width) against the bake's `sig`: their ratio sets how full the pool is. - The candle and window intensities (`3.6`, `1.5`). - The gold base colour (how much deeper than the photograph it goes). - The bake: the share of `wild` cubes sets how many lone sparks there are outside the pools. New images: segment and bake offline (tile size in px is the one parameter that matters; check the overlay), save the albedo and `-tiles.png` at the same crop and size. The data texture must fit `MAX_TEXTURE_SIZE` (4096 is safe). ## Behaviour and cost - **Draws only while something moves**: a scroll event, the pointer, the tilt, the candle easing to the pointer (~0.15 s) or the colour arriving (~0.35 s). Then the loop stops; nothing runs while idle, off screen or in a hidden tab. - One full-resolution pass (10 data reads a pixel) and five half-resolution ones. Canvas DPR capped at 2, and never finer than the photograph itself. - Assets: band 0.79 MB webp + 1.16 MB data PNG; panel 0.94 + 0.53 MB. - Without JS, without WebGL, or if the data fails to load, the `` stays. On context loss the img shows until it comes back. ## Accessibility and reduced motion - Decorative: `alt=""` on the img, the canvas is `aria-hidden`. Nothing to focus. - Touch scrolling is never touched: the canvas takes no input. - `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`: one still frame in full colour with a fixed set of glints (eye a little above the middle, candle low and left), redrawn only on resize. Scroll, pointer and tilt do nothing. - Print shows the plain image. ## Credits See `assets/credits.json`. - Justinian and his retinue, San Vitale, Ravenna (c. 547). Photograph by Ввласенко, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons. The derived tile data is shared under the same licence. - Christ, Deësis mosaic, Hagia Sophia (c. 1261). Photograph by Myrabella, public domain, Wikimedia Commons.
